Think about what an "account" is as a noun: it's a record, a report, an explanation of something. The verb "account" carries exactly that spirit — to report, explain, represent, or track something so that it is clearly understood or recorded.

In modern English, the verb almost always appears as part of the phrase "account for." This phrase has four distinct meanings, each important and common. There is also a rarer use of "account" on its own, covered at the end.

Meaning 1: To explain why something happened

This is the most common use. When you "account for" something, you provide a reason that makes it understandable. You're not just mentioning it — you're explaining it satisfactorily.

"The heavy rain accounts for the flooding in the streets."
(The rain is the reason the streets are flooded.)

"Scientists could not account for the strange results."
(They had no explanation for why the results were what they were.)

"She was asked to account for the missing money."
(She was asked to explain where the money went and why.)

Notice the sense of justification here. When you account for something, you clear it up — you make it no longer mysterious or unexplained.

Meaning 2: To make up or represent a portion of a whole

Here, "account for" means that something forms a certain share or percentage of a total. Think of it as: if you were adding up all the parts, this piece would represent that amount.

"Women account for 55% of university students."
(Women make up 55% of the total student population.)

"Sleep accounts for about one-third of our lives."
(If you divided your life into parts, sleep would take up roughly one-third of it.)

"Just five companies account for half of all profits in the industry."
(Five companies together make up half the total profit.)

This meaning is purely about proportion and contribution. There is no explanation involved — you're simply stating what share something represents.

Meaning 3: To consider or include something in your planning or calculations

In this sense, to "account for" something means to make sure you have included it in your thinking, plan, or budget. You don't overlook it; you factor it in.

"When planning the trip, make sure to account for delays."
(Include the possibility of delays in your plan; don't assume everything will go perfectly.)

"The budget doesn't account for unexpected expenses."
(The budget was made without including any allowance for unexpected costs — a gap in the planning.)

"A good engineer accounts for every possible failure point."
(A good engineer considers and prepares for every way something could go wrong.)

The key idea here is: if you fail to account for something, it was left out of your reckoning. It wasn't considered. And that omission might catch you off guard later.

Meaning 4: To confirm the location or safety of someone or something

In this use, "account for" means to establish that someone or something is known, present, or safe — to have a clear record of their status or whereabouts.

"After the fire drill, all students were accounted for."
(Every student's presence and safety was confirmed.)

"Three of the missing hikers have still not been accounted for."
(Three hikers' whereabouts or safety remain unknown — there's no record of them yet.)

"Every weapon in the armory must be accounted for."
(Every weapon must be tracked and confirmed to be in its place.)

When someone is "accounted for," they're on the record — you know where they are and that they're fine. When someone is "unaccounted for," they're missing from the record, and that's concerning.

To be answerable or report to someone (formal)

In formal or official contexts, "account" can be used without "for" to mean that someone must formally explain or justify their actions to a person or body that has authority over them.

"The police must account to the public for how they use force."
(They are obligated to explain and justify their actions to the public.)

"Government ministers are required to account to Parliament."
(They must answer to Parliament, report their actions, and justify their decisions.)

Here, to "account to" someone means to be responsible to them — not just voluntarily explaining, but being formally obligated to do so.

To consider or regard as (archaic — almost never used today)

In older English, "account" could mean "to consider" or "to regard as." You might encounter it in classic literature:

"I account him a man of great wisdom."
(I consider him, or regard him as, a wise man.)

This usage is essentially extinct in everyday modern English. You will almost never hear or read it outside of historical texts. It's worth recognising so you're not puzzled if you come across it, but you would never use it yourself in normal writing or conversation.

No matter which meaning you look at, "account" as a verb always involves some form of reckoning — keeping track of, explaining, representing, or being responsible for something. Whether you're explaining a cause, identifying what makes up a whole, including something in your planning, tracking people's safety, or formally justifying your actions to an authority, you are always providing an account of something in some shape or form. The word never strays far from that central idea of record, explanation, and responsibility.
